topic: Definition and primary vs secondary classification
candidate: Constipation = infrequent bowel movements and difficulty passing stool; intestines fail to move waste to the rectum and pelvic muscles/anal sphincter fail to coordinate. Primary (idiopathic/functional) vs secondary (medication side effect or another condition, e.g. malignancy).
main_coverage: MAIN p96: definition (infrequent BMs, difficult passage, straining, hard stools, incomplete evacuation; impaired colonic transit and/or anorectal evacuation); classification primary (functional) vs secondary (drugs, endocrine/metabolic, neurological, structural).
reason: Fully covered in MAIN, incl. structural causes under secondary.

topic: History: <3 stools/week, straining, hard stools, incomplete evacuation, bloating, manual maneuvers
candidate: History of fewer than three stools per week, straining, hard stools, feeling of incomplete evacuation, abdominal discomfort/bloating, manual maneuvers to defecate; focused history and exam including DRE mandatory.
main_coverage: MAIN p97 history list (stool frequency, consistency, straining, incomplete evacuation, manual maneuvers...); abdominal exam may reveal bloating; MAIN p3 'Constipation = >=2 of: <3 stools/week; hard stools in >1/4 of defecations'; Fig 6.1 H&P including DRE.
reason: Covered across MAIN p3, p97, p98 and Figure 6.1.

topic: Acute-onset constipation: ask about passing gas; obstipation
candidate: In acute-onset constipation always ask about the ability to pass gas: failure to pass gas can signal bowel obstruction. Obstipation = severe or complete constipation with practically no stool passage and absence of flatus, possibly with abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting; points to obstruction.
main_coverage: absent after search for: obstipation, flatus, pass gas (MAIN printed 1-197). MAIN p97 history list has 'Associated symptoms' only.
reason: Specific diagnostic clue for obstruction not stated in MAIN.
handout_text:
In acute-onset constipation, always ask whether the patient can pass gas - failure to pass gas can signal bowel obstruction.
Obstipation = severe or complete constipation with practically no stool and no flatus; it may come with abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting and points to obstruction.

topic: DRE signs of pelvic floor dyssynergia
candidate: Exam may show fecal impaction and palpable stool ball, anal fissures, hemorrhoids, or pelvic floor dyssynergia - the anal sphincter fails to relax or the perineum does not descend when the patient bears down during evacuation.
main_coverage: MAIN p98 DRE: perianal sensation and sphincter tone may identify neurological or defecatory disorders; may reveal rectal mass or palpable stool ball, anal fissures or hemorrhoids. MAIN p96 defines dyssynergia as impaired coordination of abdominal contraction and pelvic floor/sphincter relaxation. Search 'perine', 'fail to relax' found no DRE sign.
reason: Stool ball, fissures, hemorrhoids are duplicates; the bedside DRE signs of dyssynergia are incremental.
handout_text: On digital rectal examination during bearing down, pelvic floor dyssynergia is suggested when the anal sphincter fails to relax or the perineum does not descend.

topic: Red flags and colonoscopy
candidate: Red flags: hematochezia, unintentional weight loss, family history of colorectal cancer, acute onset in older adult, change in stool caliber, anemia, rectal mass -> consider colorectal cancer, colonoscopy with biopsy.
main_coverage: MAIN p97 lists identical red flags and identical action (colonoscopy with biopsy); Fig 6.1.
reason: Verbatim duplicate.

main_coverage: MAIN p98 near-verbatim identical.
reason: Verbatim duplicate.

topic: Anorectal manometry: what it measures; MRI defecography
candidate: Inadequate response -> anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion test or defecography; abnormal in defecatory disorder. Figure: anorectal manometry assesses the internal and external anal sphincters, rectal sensations and expulsion patterns; a pressure-sensitive catheter is inserted into the anorectum to measure resting and squeeze pressures of the anal canal. Image labelled 'MRI Defecography'.
main_coverage: MAIN p98 text identical ('measure pressures inside the rectum and anus and the ability of the pelvic muscles to expel stool'); Fig 6.1. Absent after search for: squeeze, resting (anal), rectal sensation, MRI defecography.
reason: Main text duplicated; the figure's specific parameters (resting/squeeze pressures, rectal sensation, both sphincters) and MRI as defecography modality are incremental.
handout_text:
Anorectal manometry uses a pressure-sensitive catheter inserted into the anorectum to measure resting and squeeze pressures of the anal canal.
It assesses the internal and external anal sphincters, rectal sensation and expulsion patterns.
Defecography can be done with MRI (MRI defecography).

topic: Colonic transit study; slow vs normal transit; IBS as normal-transit type
candidate: Normal manometry/balloon -> colonic transit study with swallowed radiopaque markers tracked by X-ray; markers not passed in expected time = slow transit; normal = normal transit constipation (disorder of gut-brain axis), one type is IBS. candidate: Functional bowel disorders: IBS, functional dyspepsia, functional chest pain of presumed esophageal origin, functional heartburn - chronic recurrent pain/discomfort referred to the lower abdomen, the epigastrium/upper abdomen and the retrosternum respectively; belong to functional GI disorders (disorders of brain-gut interaction), overlapping, common in adults and children.

topic: IBS baseline labs: CBC, ESR/CRP, TSH
candidate: Order labs to rule out other non-malignant GI conditions: CBC (anemia or infection), ESR and CRP (inflammation), TSH (thyroid dysregulation), tissue transglutaminase IgA if diarrhea (celiac), fecal calprotectin (colonic inflammation / IBD).
main_coverage: MAIN p104: 'limited laboratory investigations' - fecal calprotectin (exclude IBD), celiac serology (mainly IBS-D), colonoscopy only with alarm features. Absent in IBS section: CBC, ESR/CRP, TSH.
reason: Calprotectin and celiac serology duplicated; CBC, ESR/CRP and TSH with their purposes are incremental.
handout_text:
Besides fecal calprotectin and celiac serology (tTG IgA, for diarrhea), IM lists:
- CBC - to assess for anemia or infection
- ESR and CRP - to look for inflammation
- TSH - to assess for thyroid dysregulation

topic: Rome IV (IM) vs Rome V (MAIN) frequency threshold
candidate: IM: assess Rome IV criteria - recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, with >=2 of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form.
main_coverage: MAIN p102 (Rome V): pain on average at least 3 days per month over the last 3 months; onset >=6 months before; bothersome; same 2-of-3 associations.
reason: Frequency threshold and criteria version differ (IM p75 Rome IV '>=1 day/week' vs MAIN p102 Rome V '>=3 days/month').
handout_text:
IM p75 (Rome IV): recurrent abdominal pain on at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months.
MAIN p102 (Rome V): pain on average at least 3 days per month over the last 3 months.
The 2-of-3 associated features are the same in both. Check with your teacher which version is examined.

topic: IBS-C second drug option: linaclotide (IM) vs prucalopride (MAIN)
